newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl faces dramatic week in German EMU gold row.
newsitem.headline: Kohl faces dramatic week in German EMU gold row.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl faces a tight week of wheeling and dealing as he canvasses support for a controversial gold revaluation plan which Germany's powerful Bundesbank says he cannot use to help the country's economy qualify for the euro, the single European currency.

The plan, meant to reap 20 billion marks ($12 billion) that can partly ease Bonn's debt burden and help meet Europe's monetary union (EMU) targets, has already sparked off an unparalleled row between the government and the central bank.

Kohl and his lieutenants must now close ranks among their deputies in parliament, where weekend grumbling hinted he could fall short of the absolute majority to change the Bundesbank law and force the bank to pay out profits from revalued gold.

Analysts rank the slug-out with the Bundesbank, which last Wednesday bluntly denounced the revaluation plan as a threat to EMU and a violation of the bank's independence, among the biggest risks the chancellor has taken in his long career.

"Kohl and (Finance Minister Theo) Waigel would put themselves in really serious political danger if they tried to ignore this very clear statement by the Bundesbank," said David Marsh, European strategist at Robert Fleming in London.
Much attention will focus on Thursday, when the Bundesbank draft law goes before parliament for its first reading. The draft should be voted on before the summer break.

But a second budget battle could break out on another front when Finance Minister Theo Waigel, whose tax revenues will fall 18 billion marks ($11 billion) short of projections this year, suggests further steps to plug his budget gaps.

Kohl's small Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partner has vowed to stonewall against the two steps Waigel is expected to propose -- a rise in petrol taxes and a delay in a planned phase-out of a hated tax surcharge to rebuild eastern Germany.
"I have no doubt that we will realise our tax plans in this coalition," FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told German Radio.
Preparations for Thursday's debate on the Bundesbank law will proceed in standard Bonn fashion, with ever larger groups discussing it in private before it comes to parliament.
Kohl and his closest allies were due to meet on Sunday evening, with Waigel's budget plans also on the agenda, and the parties' parliamentary leadership groups will meet on Monday.

The chancellor is also due to address an international monetary conference in Interlaken, Switzerland on Monday, by which time the results of the French parliamentary elections will be known. No matter who wins in France, Germany's closest ally looks set to focus less on reaching EMU at any price.

The Bundesbank gold issue will then go on Tuesday to full party caucus meetings, where doubting deputies can either air their concerns or -- under massive pressure from the groups' leaders -- decide to hold their peace.

Deputies have spent the long holiday weekend in their own districts hearing voter reaction to the gold row and officials in Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) say they could come back to Bonn in a rebellious or at least very critical mood.
Germany faces a general election in late 1998 and the 14-year-old coalition is trailing opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens badly in public opinion polls.
Wednesday is normally cabinet day, but Kohl will be off in the United States commemorating the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan that helped rebuilt postwar Europe.

Instead, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who perhaps better than anyone else can sway public opinion on whether EMU will be stable or not, should hold centre stage in Bonn when he testifies before parliament's budget committee.
He is also due to dash off to Interlaken to speak to the same conference Kohl is scheduled to address on Monday.

Kohl's 342-member government coalition has only five votes more than the absolute majority needed to change the law, meaning that just a few renegades or absentees could scuttle the project. Two deputies have already come out against it.
Political sources said they would be watching first for any cracks on two fronts -- among the coalition leaders over tax hikes and among parliamentary deputies over the grab for gold.

The medium-term issue to watch will be whether German public opinion, which has long been against the euro but for Europe, will start to speak its mind more openly now that the respected Bundesbank has voiced its concerns so bluntly.

"There was always a lot of cynicism in Kohl's approach," a Bundesbank council member told Reuters recently. "He thought he could ignore popular opposition to losing the deutschemark because people were more or less resigned to it happening.
"But that high percentage of Germans expecting EMU to happen reflects frustration, not acceptance," he said.
